native_verses.46:7: He shall prepare as a grain offering an ephah for the bull and an ephah for the ram, and for the lambs as much as his hand can afford, along with a hin of oil for each ephah.
native_verses.46:8: When the prince enters, he shall enter by way of the vestibule of the gate, and by the same way he shall go out.
native_verses.46:9: But when the people of the land come before the LORD at the appointed times, whoever enters by way of the north gate to bow down in worship shall go out by way of the south gate, and whoever enters by way of the south gate shall go out by way of the north gate; he shall not return by way of the gate through which he entered, but shall go out straight ahead.
native_verses.46:10: As for the prince, he shall be in their midst: when they enter, he shall enter, and when they go out, they shall go out.
native_verses.46:11: At the festivals and at the appointed times, the grain offering shall be an ephah for each bull and an ephah for each ram, and for the lambs whatever his hand gives, along with a hin of oil for each ephah.
native_verses.46:12: When the prince prepares a freewill offering, either a burnt offering or peace offerings as a freewill offering to the LORD, the gate that faces east shall be opened for him, and he shall prepare his burnt offering and his peace offerings just as he does on the Sabbath day. Then he shall go out, and the gate shall be shut after he goes out.
native_verses.46:13: You shall also prepare a year-old lamb without blemish as a burnt offering daily to the LORD; morning by morning you shall prepare it.
native_verses.46:14: And with it you shall prepare a grain offering morning by morning: a sixth of an ephah, and a third of a hin of oil to moisten the fine flour, a grain offering to the LORD by perpetual statutes continually.
native_verses.46:15: They shall prepare the lamb, the grain offering, and the oil morning by morning as a continual burnt offering."
native_verses.46:16: This is what the Lord GOD says: "If the prince gives a gift to any of his sons, it is his inheritance; it shall belong to his sons; it is their possession by inheritance.
native_verses.46:17: But if he gives a gift from his inheritance to one of his servants, it shall be his until the year of liberty, and then it shall return to the prince; but as for his inheritance, it shall belong to his sons; it shall be theirs.
native_verses.46:18: The prince shall not take any of the people's inheritance, oppressing them out of their possession; from his own possession he shall give an inheritance to his sons, so that My people will not be scattered, each man from his possession."
native_verses.46:19: Then he brought me through the entrance that was at the side of the gate into the holy chambers for the priests, which faced north; and look, a place was there at the extreme rear toward the west.
native_verses.46:20: And he said to me, "This is the place where the priests shall boil the guilt offering and the sin offering, and where they shall bake the grain offering, so as not to bring them out into the outer court and consecrate the people."
native_verses.46:21: Then he brought me out into the outer court and led me over to the four corners of the court; and look, in every corner of the court there was a court.
native_verses.46:22: In the four corners of the court were enclosed courts, forty in length and thirty in width; these four corner courts had one measurement.
native_verses.46:23: There was a masonry row all around inside them, around all four of them, and boiling hearths were built beneath the rows all around.
native_verses.46:24: And he said to me, "These are the cooking houses where the ministers of the house shall boil the sacrifice of the people."
native_verses.47:1: Then he brought me back to the entrance of the house, and look, water was coming out from beneath the threshold of the house toward the east, for the front of the house faced east; and the water was flowing down from beneath the right side of the house, south of the altar.
native_verses.47:2: He brought me out by way of the north gate and led me around on the outside to the outer gate that faces east; and look, water was trickling out from the right side.
native_verses.47:3: As the man went out eastward with a measuring line in his hand, he measured a thousand cubits and led me through the water, water up to the ankles.
native_verses.47:4: Again he measured a thousand and led me through the water, water up to the knees. Again he measured a thousand and led me through, water up to the waist.
native_verses.47:5: Again he measured a thousand, and it was a river that I could not cross, for the water had risen, water deep enough to swim in, a river that could not be crossed.
native_verses.47:6: And he said to me, "Have you seen this, son of man?" Then he led me and brought me back to the bank of the river.
native_verses.47:7: When I returned, look, along the bank of the river were very many trees on this side and on that side.
native_verses.47:8: And he said to me, "These waters flow out toward the eastern region and go down into the Arabah; then they enter the sea, being led out into the sea, and the waters will be healed.
native_verses.47:9: And every living creature that swarms, wherever the double river goes, will live; and there will be very many fish, because these waters go there so that the waters are healed, and everything will live wherever the river goes.
native_verses.47:10: Fishermen will stand beside it from En-gedi to En-eglaim; these will be places for spreading nets. Their fish will be according to their kinds, like the fish of the Great Sea, very many.
native_verses.47:11: But its swamps and its marshes will not be healed; they will be given over to salt.
native_verses.47:12: Along the river, on its bank on this side and on that side, every kind of tree for food will grow. Its leaf will not wither and its fruit will not fail; month by month it will bear fresh fruit, because its waters flow out from the sanctuary. Its fruit will be for food, and its leaf for healing."
native_verses.47:13: This is what the Lord GOD says: "This is the boundary by which you shall divide the land as an inheritance for the twelve tribes of Israel: Joseph shall have two portions.
native_verses.47:14: You shall inherit it, each man like his brother, for I lifted My hand to give it to your fathers; and this land shall fall to you as an inheritance.
native_verses.47:15: This shall be the boundary of the land: on the north side, from the Great Sea by the way of Hethlon to the entrance of Zedad,
native_verses.47:16: Hamath, Berothah, Sibraim, which lies between the border of Damascus and the border of Hamath, and Hazer-hatticon, which is on the border of Hauran.
native_verses.47:17: Thus the boundary shall run from the sea to Hazar-enon, at the border of Damascus, and on the north, northward, is the border of Hamath. This is the north side.
native_verses.47:18: On the east side, between Hauran and Damascus, and between Gilead and the land of Israel along the Jordan, you shall measure from the boundary to the eastern sea. This is the east side.
native_verses.47:19: On the south side, southward, the boundary shall run from Tamar to the waters of Meriboth-kadesh, then along the brook to the Great Sea. This is the south side, southward.
native_verses.47:20: On the west side, the Great Sea shall be the boundary from the boundary up to a point opposite Lebo-hamath. This is the west side.
native_verses.47:21: So you shall divide this land among yourselves according to the tribes of Israel.
native_verses.47:22: You shall divide it by lot as an inheritance for yourselves and for the sojourners who sojourn in your midst, who have fathered children in your midst. They shall be to you like the native-born among the sons of Israel; with you they shall receive an allotment by lot as an inheritance among the tribes of Israel.
native_verses.47:23: In whatever tribe the sojourner sojourns, there you shall assign his inheritance," declares the Lord GOD.
native_verses.48:1: Now these are the names of the tribes: From the northern end, alongside the road of Hethlon to Lebo-hamath, Hazar-enan, the boundary of Damascus northward alongside Hamath, the eastern side and the west shall belong to him: Dan, one share.
native_verses.48:2: And along the boundary of Dan, from the eastern side to the western side: Asher, one share.
native_verses.48:3: And along the boundary of Asher, from the eastern side to the western side: Naphtali, one share.
native_verses.48:4: And along the boundary of Naphtali, from the eastern side to the western side: Manasseh, one share.
native_verses.48:5: And along the boundary of Manasseh, from the eastern side to the western side: Ephraim, one share.
native_verses.48:6: And along the boundary of Ephraim, from the eastern side to the western side: Reuben, one share.
native_verses.48:7: And along the boundary of Reuben, from the eastern side to the western side: Judah, one share.
native_verses.48:8: And along the boundary of Judah, from the eastern side to the western side, shall be the contribution that you are to set apart: twenty-five thousand in width, and in length like one of the shares, from the eastern side to the western side; and the sanctuary shall be in the middle of it.
native_verses.48:9: The contribution that you are to set apart to the LORD shall be twenty-five thousand in length and ten thousand in width.
native_verses.48:10: And to these shall belong the holy contribution, to the priests: on the north twenty-five thousand, and on the west ten thousand in width, and on the east ten thousand in width, and on the south twenty-five thousand in length; and the sanctuary of the LORD shall be in the middle of it.
native_verses.48:11: This shall belong to the consecrated priests from the sons of Zadok, who kept My charge, who did not stray when the sons of Israel strayed, just as the Levites strayed.
native_verses.48:12: And it shall belong to them as a dedicated contribution from the contribution of the land, most holy, next to the boundary of the Levites.
native_verses.48:13: And parallel to the boundary of the priests, the Levites shall have twenty-five thousand in length and ten thousand in width; the entire length shall be twenty-five thousand, and the width ten thousand.
native_verses.48:14: And they shall not sell any of it, nor shall anyone exchange it, nor shall anyone transfer the best of the land, for it is holy to the LORD.
native_verses.48:15: And the five thousand remaining in width, fronting the twenty-five thousand, shall be unconsecrated, for the city, for dwellings and for open land; and the city shall be in the middle of it.
native_verses.48:16: And these are its measurements: the northern side, four thousand five hundred; and the southern side, four thousand five hundred; and on the eastern side, four thousand five hundred; and the western side, four thousand five hundred.
native_verses.48:17: And the city shall have open land: on the north, two hundred fifty; on the south, two hundred fifty; on the east, two hundred fifty; and on the west, two hundred fifty.
native_verses.48:18: And what remains in length, parallel to the holy contribution, shall be ten thousand to the east and ten thousand to the west, and it shall be parallel to the holy contribution; and its produce shall be for food for those who serve the city.
native_verses.48:19: And those from all the tribes of Israel who serve the city shall work it.
native_verses.48:20: The entire contribution shall be twenty-five thousand by twenty-five thousand; as a square you shall set apart the holy contribution along with the possession of the city.
native_verses.48:21: And what remains shall belong to the prince, on both sides of the holy contribution and of the possession of the city, fronting the twenty-five thousand of the contribution as far as the eastern boundary, and on the west fronting the twenty-five thousand to the western boundary, parallel to the shares; it shall belong to the prince. And the holy contribution and the sanctuary of the house shall be in the middle of it.
native_verses.48:22: And apart from the possession of the Levites and the possession of the city, which shall be in the middle of what belongs to the prince, what lies between the boundary of Judah and the boundary of Benjamin shall belong to the prince.
native_verses.48:23: And the remaining tribes: from the eastern side to the western side, Benjamin, one share.
native_verses.48:24: And along the boundary of Benjamin, from the eastern side to the western side: Simeon, one share.
native_verses.48:25: And along the boundary of Simeon, from the eastern side to the western side: Issachar, one share.
native_verses.48:26: And along the boundary of Issachar, from the eastern side to the western side: Zebulun, one share.
native_verses.48:27: And along the boundary of Zebulun, from the eastern side to the western side: Gad, one share.
native_verses.48:28: And along the boundary of Gad, on the southern side southward, the boundary shall run from Tamar to the waters of Meribath-kadesh, to the brook, to the Great Sea.
native_verses.48:29: This is the land that you shall assign by lot as an inheritance to the tribes of Israel, and these are their divisions, declares the Lord GOD.
native_verses.48:30: And these are the exits of the city: on the northern side, four thousand five hundred in measurement.
native_verses.48:31: And the gates of the city shall bear the names of the tribes of Israel, three gates on the north: the gate of Reuben, one; the gate of Judah, one; the gate of Levi, one.
native_verses.48:32: And on the eastern side, four thousand five hundred, and three gates: the gate of Joseph, one; the gate of Benjamin, one; the gate of Dan, one.
native_verses.48:33: And on the southern side, four thousand five hundred in measurement, and three gates: the gate of Simeon, one; the gate of Issachar, one; the gate of Zebulun, one.
native_verses.48:34: On the western side, four thousand five hundred; their gates are three: the gate of Gad, one; the gate of Asher, one; the gate of Naphtali, one.
native_verses.48:35: All around, it shall be eighteen thousand; and from that day onward the name of the city shall be "The LORD Is There."

native_notes.1:4: The rare noun chashmal (occurring only in Ezek 1:4, 27; 8:2) likely denotes a luminous metal alloy such as electrum (cf. Akkadian elmeshu). The construct noun 'en (lit. 'eye') is used throughout chapter 1 for 'gleam' or 'luster,' and the Hithpael participle mithlaqqachat conveys fire continuously flaring back and forth.
native_notes.1:5: Throughout Ezekiel 1, masculine and feminine plural pronouns and suffixes alternate freely when referring to the four living creatures (chayyoth, grammatically feminine) and their parts.
native_notes.1:8: Ketiv/Qere: the Qere (read form) is widey ('and hands of'), whereas the Ketiv (written form) is wydw ('and his hand').
native_notes.1:15: Literally 'for its four faces'; the masculine singular suffix on panaw apparently refers distributively to each four-faced creature (or to the four fronts of the group).
native_notes.1:23: The Hebrew text repeats the clause 'each had two covering them,' likely emphasizing the paired wings covering each creature's body on both sides.
native_notes.2:2: The noun ruach ("spirit") lacks the definite article here (as also in 3:12, 14, 24; 8:3; 11:1, 24; 43:5) and can denote "a spirit," "the Spirit," or "wind." The participle middabber ("the One speaking") is a rare Hithpael form of dabar with assimilated taw.
native_notes.2:6: Sarabim ('briers') is a hapax legomenon, traditionally understood alongside sallonim ('thorns') as thorny briers or stubborn resisters.
native_notes.2:10: Hi ('woe') occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible, likely a shortened form of nehi ('wailing') or an exclamation of grief.
native_notes.3:5: Literally 'deep of lip and heavy of tongue,' a Hebrew idiom for people who speak an obscure, foreign language (cf. Isa 33:19).
native_notes.3:6: The particle 'im-lo' ('surely') introduces an emphatic statement with implied conditional force: if Ezekiel were sent to foreign nations, they would listen.
native_notes.3:12: Hebrew ruach lacks the definite article here and may be read as "a spirit," "the Spirit," or "wind" (cf. 2:2). The Masoretic Text reads barukh ('blessed be'), preserved here without textual emendation.
native_notes.3:14: Hebrew ruach ("a spirit") lacks the definite article here and may be read as "a spirit," "the Spirit," or "wind" (cf. 2:2).
native_notes.3:15: Ketiv/Qere: the Qere (read form) is wa'eshev ('and I dwelt/sat'), translated here as 'and I dwelt where they were dwelling,' whereas the Ketiv (written form) is wa'asher ('and where').
native_notes.3:24: Hebrew ruach lacks the definite article here and may be read as "a spirit," "the Spirit," or "wind" (cf. 2:2).
native_notes.4:6: Ketiv/Qere: Ketiv reads הימיני (hayyemini), while Qere reads הַיְמָנִי (hayyemani); both are spelling variants of the adjective meaning "right."
native_notes.4:10: The Hebrew idiom מֵעֵת עַד־עֵת literally means "from time to time," denoting fixed daily intervals (repeated in 4:11).
native_notes.4:12: The verb תְּעֻגֶנָה (Qal imperfect 2ms of the rare denominative root עוג with a 3fs suffix) forms a wordplay with עֻגַת ("cake"), meaning "you shall bake it as a cake."
native_notes.4:15: Ketiv/Qere: Ketiv reads צפועי, while Qere reads צְפִיעֵי, both spelling variants of a rare noun denoting cattle dung.
native_notes.5:7: Hebrew הֲמָנְכֶם (from הָמוֹן/המה, "tumult, commotion, turbulence") refers to unruly commotion; also, the Masoretic Text includes לֹא ("not") in the final clause, implying Israel failed to live up even to the surrounding nations' standards (contrast Ezek 11:12).
native_notes.5:11: Hebrew אֶגְרַע (Qal imperfect of גרע, "diminish, withdraw," or "shear/clip off" as in Isa 15:2) appears here without an explicit object, hence rendered "withdraw."
native_notes.5:13: Hebrew וְהִנֶּחָמְתִּי is a Hithpael weqatal of נחם with assimilated taw, conveying the sense of relieving oneself of anger or finding satisfaction.
native_notes.5:15: The Masoretic Text uses the 3rd-person feminine singular verb וְהָיְתָה ("and she will become," referring to Jerusalem) before resuming 2nd-person feminine singular address (סְבִיבוֹתָיִךְ, "around you"); similarly, 5:16 shifts from 3rd-person plural בָּהֶם ("against them") to 2nd-person plural לְשַׁחֶתְכֶם ("to destroy you").
native_notes.6:3: Ketiv/Qere: Ketiv reads ולגיאות, while Qere reads וְלַגֵּיאָיוֹת ("and to the valleys"), a variant plural spelling of גַּיְא ("valley").
native_notes.6:6: Hebrew וְיֶאְשְׁמוּ (Qal imperfect of אשׁם, "bear guilt" or "suffer the penalty of guilt") forms a soundplay with תִּישָׁמְנָה (Qal imperfect of ישׁם, "become desolate") earlier in the verse.
native_notes.6:9: Hebrew נִשְׁבַּרְתִּי (Niphal perfect 1cs of שׁבר, "I have been broken") is unusually followed by the marker אֶת before "their heart" and "their eyes," expressing the cause or respect in which the LORD was broken.
native_notes.6:14: Hebrew מִמִּדְבַּר דִּבְלָתָה combines the construct noun מִדְבַּר with directional דִּבְלָתָה ("from the wilderness to Diblah," or "more than the wilderness toward Diblah"). Diblah is otherwise unknown and is often compared to Riblah in northern Syria due to the graphic similarity of ד and ר.
native_notes.7:2: Ketiv ארבעת (feminine construct) vs. Qere אַרְבַּע (masculine construct, standard before feminine כַּנְפוֹת, literally 'wings' or 'edges').
native_notes.7:3: Native Masoretic order places 7:3–5 before 7:6–9. In the Saints.Bible parallel display, MT 7:6–9 map to slots 7:3–6, MT 7:3–4 map to slots 7:7–8, and MT 7:5 is combined with 7:10 at slot 7:10 (leaving slot 7:9 unmapped).
native_notes.7:7: הַצְּפִירָה ('the doom', also in 7:10) is a rare noun meaning 'cycle/turn of fate' or 'doom' (compare 'crown/wreath' in Isa 28:5); הֵד is a hapax legomenon related to הֵידָד ('joyful shouting').
native_notes.7:10: Native Masoretic order preserves MT 7:3–5 before 7:6–9 and 7:10 as a standalone verse. In the Saints.Bible parallel display, MT 7:6–9 appear at slots 7:3–6, MT 7:3–4 at slots 7:7–8, there is no separate slot 7:9, and MT 7:5 ('This is what the Lord GOD says: Disaster, a singular disaster! Look, it is coming!') is combined with MT 7:10 at slot 7:10.
native_notes.7:11: Contains two hapax legomena of uncertain sense in elliptical verbless clauses: מֶהֱמֵהֶם ('of their abundance/wealth', or 'tumult') and נֹהַּ ('eminence/preeminence', or possibly 'wailing' from נהה).
native_notes.7:21: Ketiv וחללוה (third-person feminine singular suffix) vs. Qere וְחִלְּלוּהוּ (third-person masculine singular suffix, referring back to the masculine 'beauty of its ornament' in 7:20).
native_notes.8:2: The Masoretic Hebrew reads אֵשׁ ('fire', compare 1:27), whereas the Septuagint reflects אִישׁ ('a man'); הַחַשְׁמַלָה ('glowing metal', with paragogic -ah) is a rare term confined to Ezekiel (1:4, 27; 8:2) denoting glowing metal, electrum, or amber.
native_notes.8:3: Hebrew ruach lacks the definite article here and may be read as "a spirit," "the Spirit," or "wind" (cf. 2:2).
native_notes.8:6: Ketiv מהם (written as one word) vs. Qere מָה הֵם ('what they'); the Qal infinitive construct לְרׇחֳקָה ('to go far away') implies causing God to depart far from His sanctuary.
native_notes.8:11: עֲתַר is a hapax legomenon, understood either as 'aroma/fragrance' or as a 'thick, billowing mass' of incense smoke.
native_notes.8:16: מִשְׁתַּחֲוִיתֶם is an anomalous conflate Masoretic form combining the Hishtaphel participle מִשְׁתַּחֲוִים ('bowing down') with a second-person plural ending -tem.
native_notes.8:17: 'Extending the branch to their nose' describes an obscure gesture of cultic provocation; Jewish scribal tradition lists אַפָּם ('their nose') among the tiqqunei soferim ('emendations of the scribes') for an original 'My nose'.
native_notes.9:1: קָרְבוּ is vocalized as a Qal perfect ('have drawn near'), though with different vocalization (קִרְבוּ or קַרְּבוּ) it is often read as an imperative ('Draw near' or 'Bring near'); פְּקֻדּוֹת ('visitations/punishments') is used concretely for the appointed executioners.
native_notes.9:5: Two Ketiv/Qere variants: Ketiv על ('upon' or orthographic variant) vs. Qere אַל ('do not'), and Ketiv עיניכם (plural 'your eyes') vs. Qere עֵינְכֶם (singular 'your eye', matching the feminine singular verb תָּחֹס).
native_notes.9:8: וְנֵאשְׁאַר is an anomalous conflate Masoretic form blending the first-person singular imperfect אֶשָּׁאֵר and the Niphal participle נִשְׁאָר ('I was left').
native_notes.9:9: מֻטֶּה is a hapax legomenon from the root נטה ('bend, turn aside'), denoting 'perverted justice' or 'injustice'.
native_notes.9:11: Ketiv כאשר ('just as') vs. Qere כְּכֹל אֲשֶׁר ('according to all that').
native_notes.10:2: Heb. haggalgal ("the wheelwork") is a singular collective noun for the rolling wheel assembly, distinguished from the plural ʾopannim ("wheels") in vv. 9-13. Heb. chofnekha is dual, denoting both cupped hands.
native_notes.10:9: Heb. ʾeven tarshish is literally "stone of Tarshish," a precious stone commonly identified as beryl or chrysolite.
native_notes.10:12: Heb. gabbehem denotes "their backs" here alongside body, hands, and wings (the same noun denotes wheel "rims" in 1:18). The final appositional phrase leʾarbaʿtam ʾopannehem literally reads "for the four of them, their wheels."
native_notes.10:19: MT reads the singular verb wayyaʿamod ("and it stood"), treating the cherubim and wheels together as a single unit or resuming "the glory of the LORD" from v. 18.
native_notes.11:1: Hebrew ruach lacks the definite article here and may be read as "a spirit," "the Spirit," or "wind" (cf. 2:2).
native_notes.11:7: MT reads the Hiphil third-person masculine singular hotsiʾ (used impersonally, "one will bring out," hence "you will be brought out"), contrasting with the first-person "I will bring you out" in v. 9.
native_notes.11:15: Heb. ʾanshe geʾullatekha is literally "the men of your redemption," referring to relatives bound by the obligation of kinsman-redemption (compare Lev 25:25).
native_notes.11:16: Heb. miqdash meʿat can mean either "a sanctuary in small measure" or temporally "a sanctuary for a little while" during the exile.
native_notes.11:19: MT abruptly shifts to a second-person plural suffix in beqirbekhem ("within you") amid the surrounding third-person plural pronouns ("them," "their"), continuing the alternation of address from vv. 16-18.
native_notes.11:21: MT reads weʾel-lev shiqqutsehem ("toward the heart of their detestable things"), an unusual expression pairing the people's "heart" with the "heart" (core or desire) of their detestable practices.
native_notes.11:24: The first occurrence of ruach lacks the definite article ("a spirit," though "the Spirit" or "wind" is also plausible; cf. 2:2), whereas the second stands in construct with God (beruach elohim, "by the Spirit of God").
native_notes.12:10: The Hebrew verbless clause fronts "the prince" (הַנָּשִׂיא) without a preposition before "this burden" (הַמַּשָּׂא הַזֶּה), creating a wordplay between prophetic "burden/oracle" (מַשָּׂא) and "carry" (נָשָׂא, vv. 6-7, 12). The final suffix in בְתוֹכָם is literally 3rd-person masculine plural ("in their midst").
native_notes.12:12: The conjunction יַעַן אֲשֶׁר (normally causal, "because") functions here with purpose or result force ("so that"), accompanied by the emphatic pronoun הוּא ("he himself") and לַעַיִן (lit. "to/with the eye").
native_notes.12:19: Verses 19-20 weave a threefold wordplay on the root שׁמם: drinking "with horror" (בְּשִׁמָּמוֹן), "her land" (Jerusalem's) "will be desolated" (תֵּשַׁם), and the land becoming "a desolation" (שְׁמָמָה, v. 20).
native_notes.12:25: The Niphal imperfect תִמָּשֵׁךְ ("be drawn out / postponed") is 3rd-person feminine singular, used impersonally here and again in v. 28 with the masculine plural subject כׇּל־דְּבָרָי ("all My words").
native_notes.13:3: The negative particle לְבִלְתִּי, ordinarily used with an infinitive construct, governs the finite Qal perfect verb רָאוּ ("and have seen nothing"), a rare biblical construction.
native_notes.13:11: The Masoretic Text reads the 2nd-person feminine plural pronoun וְאַתֵּנָה ("and you, hailstones, will fall"), addressing the hailstones (אַבְנֵי אֶלְגָּבִישׁ) directly in apostrophe rather than reading a 1st-person verb ("I will send") as in some ancient versions.
native_notes.13:14: After masculine singular suffixes referring to the wall (וְהִגַּעְתִּיהוּ, יְסֹדוֹ), the Hebrew shifts abruptly to feminine singular in וְנָפְלָה ("she/it will fall") and בְּתוֹכָהּ ("in her/its midst"), pointing through the metaphor to the city of Jerusalem (cf. v. 16).
native_notes.13:18: The rare nouns כְּסָתוֹת ("bands," also v. 20) and מִסְפָּחוֹת ("veils," also v. 21) refer to arm bindings and head coverings used in divinatory rituals. MT's אַצִּילֵי יָדַי literally reads "joints of my hands," generally understood as a shortened dual for "joints of hands" (wrists) parallel to "the head of every stature."
native_notes.13:20: The Qal feminine plural participle לְפֹרְחוֹת ("like birds") reflects the late Hebrew and Aramaic sense of פרח ("fly"). The resumptive object אֶת־נְפָשִׁים preserves an unusual masculine-ending plural of נֶפֶשׁ (elsewhere נְפָשׁוֹת).
native_notes.14:3: The phrase "brought up their idols upon their heart" reflects the Hiphil of alah (lit. "cause to ascend"), portraying deliberate devotion to idolatry. The verb form ha-iddarosh iddaresh pairs a rare Niphal infinitive absolute (with prosthetic aleph assimilated from the following verb) with a tolerative Niphal imperfect of darash, emphasizing "Should I truly allow Myself to be inquired of?"
native_notes.14:4: Ketiv reads bh ("by it" or "in the matter"), whereas Qere reads ba ("coming," Qal participle of bo), translated here as "who comes." Both v. 4 and v. 7 use the Niphal of anah ("answer, respond") to stress that the LORD Himself will respond directly.
native_notes.14:8: The unusual verb form vahashimotihu combines the sin consonant of sim ("make, set") with the geminate Hiphil vocalization of shamem ("appall, devastate"), followed by the idiom "into a sign and bywords" (plural meshalim).
native_notes.14:14: Ketiv writes the name defectively as dn'l ("Danel") here and in v. 20, while Qere reads Daniyyel ("Daniel"). The verb yenatselu ("would rescue") is a rare Piel of natsal, contrasting with the standard Hiphil yatsilu in vv. 16, 18, and 20.
native_notes.14:17: Because cherev ("sword") is feminine singular, the 3fs verb taavor is translated as a jussive statement, "Let a sword pass through the land," rather than a second-person direct address.
native_notes.15:2: The comparative idiom mah-yihyeh ... mikkol-ets literally asks "what is [the wood of the vine] more than any wood?" The feminine noun hazzemorah ("the vine branch") stands in apposition to masculine ets-haggefen ("the wood of the vine"), which accounts for the masculine verb hayah ("is") that follows.
native_notes.15:3: In vv. 3 and 5, the verb asah ("make, work") combined with limlakhah ("for work") denotes working or employing a material for a useful craft or object.
native_notes.15:4: The Hebrew repeats the root akhal ("eat, consume") across vv. 4-7, pairing the noun leokhlah ("to be consumed," lit. "for food/consumption," vv. 4, 6) with the fire consuming the wood and the inhabitants of Jerusalem (vv. 4, 5, 7). Both nachar (v. 4) and vayyechar (v. 5) are Niphal forms of charar ("be charred, scorched").
native_notes.16:4: The noun translated "for cleansing" is a Hebrew hapax legomenon whose exact etymology is uncertain, generally understood from cognate roots as cleansing or rubbing smooth. The final two clauses pair a Hophal infinitive absolute with a passive verb (Hophal of malach, Pual of chatal) for emphatic negation.
native_notes.16:13: Following the qere ("fine linen" and "you ate"); the ketiv writes "my fine linen" (or a variant spelling) and an archaic second-person feminine singular ending (-ti) on the verb, a ketiv/qere pattern that recurs on the verbs in vv. 18, 22, and 31.
native_notes.16:16: The closing Hebrew clause is notably terse, literally "not coming things and it will not be," expressing unprecedented outrage.
native_notes.16:20: Following the qere plural ("your acts of prostitution"); the ketiv is singular ("your prostitution"), a variant that recurs in v. 25. In v. 21, the Hiphil of avar ("causing them to pass over") is the technical Hebrew idiom for child sacrifice by fire, though "fire" is unstated here.
native_notes.16:29: Hebrew eretz kenaan literally means "land of Canaan," playing on v. 3 while using kenaan in its secondary sense of "commerce" or "merchants" for Chaldea (compare 17:4).
native_notes.16:36: The noun translated "lust" (nechoshet) is uncertain in meaning, elsewhere denoting "bronze," and is commonly understood here from Akkadian cognates as sexual passion or lavishly spent wealth.
native_notes.16:43: Following the qere on both verbs (standard 2fs forms where the ketiv writes the archaic -ti ending, as also in vv. 47 and 51). The final negative clause (velo asit) is rendered as an unmarked rhetorical question matching the Qal perfect verb.
native_notes.16:51: Following the qere plural ("your sisters") where the ketiv consonantal spelling could be read singular; the verse also has the archaic -ti ketiv ending on the final verb.
native_notes.16:53: The idiom "restore the fortunes" pairs the verb shuv with shevit/shevut, where the qere reads shevut three times against the ketiv shevit. The closing phrase combines both nouns (shevut shevitayikh) emphatically.
native_notes.16:59: Following the qere 1cs verb ("I will deal"); the ketiv omits the final yod. In v. 57, the Hebrew text reads "Aram" (Syria), translated literally rather than emended to "Edom."
native_notes.17:4: Hebrew אֶרֶץ כְּנַעַן ("land of Canaan") functions here as a wordplay on the sense of כְּנַעַן as "merchant" or "trade," parallel to עִיר רֹכְלִים ("city of merchants"), referring to Babylon.
native_notes.17:5: קָח is a rare form of לקח ("took") lacking the initial lamed; צַפְצָפָה ("willow") is a hapax legomenon, identified via Semitic cognates (cf. Arabic safsaf) as a water-loving willow.
native_notes.17:9: יְקוֹסֵס ("strip off") is a hapax Poel imperfect of the geminate root קסס, and לְמַשְׂאוֹת ("to pull it up") is a rare Aramaizing Qal infinitive construct of נשׂא with a mem prefix.
native_notes.17:21: MT מִבְרָחָו ("his fugitives," from ברח, "flee") shows a defective spelling of the plural suffix -āw and is preceded by the marker אֵת before the grammatical subject.
native_notes.18:10: MT וְעָשָׂה אָח מֵאַחַד מֵאֵלֶּה is syntactically compressed, literally "and does [to] a brother from one of these" (compare אָח in v. 18); some interpreters alternatively take אָח as meaning "the like of" any one of these offenses.
native_notes.18:14: וַיִּרְאֶה is an unapocopated Qal wayyiqtol of ראה ("see, consider"), appearing again in v. 28; some ancient versions instead read a form of ירא ("fear").
native_notes.18:17: MT reads מֵעָנִי ("from the poor," i.e., refraining from harming the poor), in contrast to מֵעָוֶל ("from injustice") in v. 8.
native_notes.18:20: Qere reads definite הָרָשָׁע ("the wicked one," matching definite הַצַּדִּיק, "the righteous one"), whereas ketiv writes anarthrous רשע.
native_notes.18:28: Qere reads the standard apocopated Qal wayyiqtol וַיָּשָׁב ("and turns back"), whereas ketiv writes the long form וישוב.
native_notes.19:5: נוֹחֲלָה is a Niphal perfect 3fs of יחל ("wait, hope"), denoting prolonged waiting in vain, parallel to אָבְדָה תִּקְוָתָהּ ("her hope had perished").
native_notes.19:7: MT וַיֵּדַע אַלְמְנוֹתָיו literally reads "he knew [i.e., violated] his/their widows" (with 3ms collective suffix referring to אָדָם in v. 6); many compare אַלְמְנוֹתָיו to the l/r by-form of אַרְמְנוֹתָיו ("citadels, fortresses") in Isa 13:22, parallel to "their cities."
native_notes.19:9: סוּגַר ("cage") is a hapax legomenon, cognate with Akkadian shigaru, denoting a wooden neck-stock, collar, or cage used to confine wild beasts or royal captives.
native_notes.19:10: MT reads בְּדָמְךָ ("in your blood," possibly meaning "in your bloodline" or "in your vigor"); a conjectural emendation reads בְּכַרְמְךָ ("in your vineyard").
native_notes.20:5: Hebrew "lifted My hand" (nasa yad) is a gesture and idiom for swearing a solemn oath, recurring throughout the chapter (20:6, 15, 23, 28, 42).
native_notes.20:26: The Hebrew phrase "cause everything that opens the womb to pass over" uses the Hiphil of abar (echoing Exod 13:12) and implicitly refers to child sacrifice by fire (explicit in 20:31). The Hiphil verb ashimmem (from shamem) can mean either "appall" or "devastate."
native_notes.20:29: The Hebrew contains a wordplay linking bamah ("high place," transliterated Bamah) with mah ("what") and baim ("going"), mocking the illegitimate cultic shrines.
native_notes.20:37: The noun masoret ("bond") occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible and is generally derived from asar ("to bind"), denoting the binding obligation of the covenant.
native_notes.20:39: The Hebrew syntax of the middle clause is terse and elliptical: literally "and afterward, if you are not listening to Me," which can also be read as an oath-like assertion meaning "and afterward you will surely listen to Me."
native_notes.21:2: The verse uses three Hebrew terms for south (Teman, Darom, and Negev); "drop words" translates the Hiphil imperative of nataph ("drip"), an idiom for prophetic utterance.
native_notes.21:15: The Hebrew of the second half ("Or shall we rejoice? The scepter of My son despises every tree") is famously cryptic, with the feminine participle mo'eset ("despising") linking either to "scepter" or to the feminine "sword"; the same phrase recurs in verse 18.
native_notes.21:20: Hebrew ibchat ("threat" or "slaughter") is a hapax legomenon of uncertain meaning, and me'uttah is the Pual participle of 'atah ("wrapped"), sometimes understood as a variant for "polished."
native_notes.21:28: Ketiv reads kqswm (plene spelling) while Qere reads kiqsam ("like divining" in construct with shav', "falsehood"), which is translated here. The phrase "bound as they are by solemn oaths" translates the rare Qal passive participle construct shevu'ei followed by shevu'ot ("oaths").
native_notes.21:33: Hebrew lehakhil is the Hiphil infinitive construct of kul (literally "to contain" or "to hold"), used idiomatically for "to the utmost" and often understood by ancient versions as "to consume."
native_notes.22:16: Hebrew wenichalt is vocalized as the Niphal of chalal ("you will be profaned"), meaning Jerusalem will suffer desecration in herself before the nations, rather than the Qal of nachal ("inherit").
native_notes.22:18: Ketiv reads lesug while Qere reads lesig ("for dross"), matching the plural sigim ("dross") later in this verse and in verse 19; the Qere is translated here.
native_notes.22:24: Hebrew gushmah is an unusual Masoretic form combining a passive verbal vocalization of gasham ("rained upon") with a final mappiq-he (as if a suffixed noun, "her rain"); the sense in context is that the land receives no rain in the day of indignation.
native_notes.22:25: The Masoretic Text reads qesher nevi'eha ("a conspiracy of her prophets"), which is followed here rather than the Septuagint's "her princes."
native_notes.23:5: MT qerovim (also v. 12) is the plural of qarov ("near, nearby"), referring to Assyrian officials stationed in neighboring territories; some scholars instead link it to Aramaic or Akkadian roots meaning "warriors." Hebrew tachtai literally means "under Me," an idiom for being under a husband's authority.
native_notes.23:21: Follows the Masoretic text directly: ba'asot (Qal infinitive construct of 'asah II, "handle, fondle," cf. Piel in vv. 3, 8) with partitive mi-Mitsrayim ("those from Egypt") and lema'an ("on account of").
native_notes.23:24: Hebrew hotsen occurs only here in the Bible and is traditionally understood as "weapons" or "armaments."
native_notes.23:42: Follows the Qere ("Sabeans"); the Ketiv reads sove'im (Qal participle of sava', "drunkards").
native_notes.23:43: Follows the Qere 'attah yiznu ("now they will practice prostitution," Qal imperfect 3mp of zanah); the Ketiv reads 'et ("time") and yizneh (3ms). The terse final word vehi literally reads "and she."
native_notes.24:2: Ketiv/Qere orthographic variant: the ketiv is spelled plene (ktwb) and the qere defectively (ktb) before the maqqef; both represent the Qal masculine singular imperative of katav ("write").
native_notes.24:5: MT reads "the bones" (ha-atsamim), not "the wood" (ha-etsim), maintaining the stark imagery of the pot; the preceding laqoach ("take") is a Qal infinitive absolute used imperatively.
native_notes.24:12: The opening clause te'unim hel'at ("she has exhausted efforts") is notably terse and preserves the archaic third-person feminine singular Hiphil ending -at on la'ah ("weary, exhaust"). The closing verbless clause be'esh chel'atah ("into the fire with her corrosion!") may alternatively indicate that her corrosion will not come out even by fire.
native_notes.24:14: MT reads the third-person plural Qal perfect shefatukh ("they will judge you," an indefinite plural or reference to the Babylonian invaders), rather than first-person singular "I will judge you."
native_notes.24:22: Within Ezekiel's recounting of the LORD's message, the voice briefly shifts in verses 22-23 into Ezekiel's own first-person perspective ("as I have done") before returning to third-person reference to Ezekiel in verse 24. "The bread of men" (also in v. 17) refers to consolation food customarily brought to mourners.
native_notes.25:7: Ketiv/Qere variant: the qere reads levaz ("as plunder," matching 26:5), whereas the ketiv reads levag (either a rare loanword for "food/portion" or a scribal confusion of gimel and zayin).
native_notes.25:9: Ketiv/Qere variant: the qere reads the dual place-name ve-Qiryataymah ("and Kiriathaim," with final -ah), whereas the ketiv wqrytmh omits the yod.
native_notes.25:16: The Hebrew employs a wordplay between the Hiphil verb vehikhratti ("and I will cut off," root krt) and the gentilic name Keretim ("Cherethites").
native_notes.26:7: The Hebrew spells the Babylonian king's name Nevukhadretstsar (closer to Akkadian Nabu-kudurri-usur), rendered here with the standard English spelling Nebuchadnezzar.
native_notes.26:9: The phrase mechi qavollo ("the blow of his battering ram") consists of two hapax legomena from roots meaning "strike" and "be opposite/in front." "His axes" renders charvotav, literally "his swords" or "iron blades," here iron demolition tools (cf. Exod 20:25).
native_notes.26:17: MT reads the Niphal participle noshevet miyyammim ("inhabited from the seas," i.e., populated by seafaring peoples) and repeats yosheveha ("her inhabitants") at the close of the verse, referring to the inhabitants of the surrounding maritime region or Tyre's dependencies.
native_notes.26:20: MT reads venatatti tsevi be'erets chayyim ("and I will set glory in the land of the living"), contrasting Tyre's descent to the pit with God's establishment of splendor among the living.
native_notes.27:3: Ketiv hyšbty preserves an archaic feminine participle ending (-i), while Qere hayyōšebet is the standard Qal active participle feminine singular ("who sits"); the translation follows the Qere.
native_notes.27:6: MT bat-ʾăšurîm (literally "daughter of boxwoods") is widely understood as a word-division variant for bĕtaʾăšurîm ("in boxwood," cf. Isa 41:19; 60:13).
native_notes.27:15: Ketiv whwbnm and Qere wĕhobnîm ("and ebony") are orthographic variants of the same plural noun; the translation follows the Qere.
native_notes.27:17: Hebrew pannag is a hapax legomenon of uncertain meaning, likely referring to a type of fine meal or baked confection (cf. Akkadian pannigu).
native_notes.27:19: MT wĕdān may be read either as the Arabian place name "Vedan" or as "and Dan," and mĕʾuzzāl either as "from Uzal" (cf. Gen 10:27) or as a Pual participle meaning "spun yarn."
native_notes.28:3: Ketiv mdnʾl spells the name defectively ("Danel"), while Qere middānîyyēʾl reads the standard form "Daniel"; the translation follows the Qere.
native_notes.28:12: MT ḥōtēm tāknît uses the Qal active participle of ḥātam ("sealing up") with tāknît ("proportion, measurement," cf. 43:10), conveying "one who sets the seal on perfection"; many also take ḥōtēm as a construct form of ḥōtām ("seal/signet of perfection").
native_notes.28:13: The phrase tuppêkā ûnĕqābêkā literally refers to "your tambourines" (tōp) and "your pipes" or "perforations" (neqeb, a hapax common noun from nāqab, "to pierce"), though in proximity to gold and gemstones it is often interpreted as jewelry "settings and sockets."
native_notes.28:14: MT reads ʾatt-kĕrûb mimšaḥ hassōkēk ("You were an anointed, overshadowing cherub"), using the defective spelling ʾatt for the masculine singular pronoun "you" (cf. Num 11:15; Deut 5:27) rather than the preposition "with" (ʾēt); the hapax noun mimšaḥ is usually derived from māšaḥ ("anoint"), though some connect it to an Aramaic cognate meaning "outstretched."
native_notes.28:16: MT wāʾabbedkā is a Piel first-person singular wayyiqtol of ʾābad ("and I destroyed you") with contracted initial ʾālep, addressing the cherub directly.
native_notes.29:3: Hebrew tannim is a singular spelling variant of tannin, referring to a great aquatic monster or chaos dragon. The verb asitini, Qal perfect 1cs with a 1cs suffix, is translated here as a dative suffix meaning made it for myself, parallel to 29:9, though it can also be read reflexively as I made myself.
native_notes.29:4: Follows the qere hachim, hooks, rather than the ketiv spelling hachayim.
native_notes.29:7: Follows the qere bakkaf, with the hand, rather than the ketiv bekappekha, by your hand. The final verb wehaamadta is a Hiphil of amad, literally bring to a standstill; many scholars see metathesis for the root maad, cause to shake, as in Psalm 69:24.
native_notes.29:10: Migdol lay near Egypt's northeastern frontier and Syene, Hebrew Seveneh with a directional suffix meaning to Syene, lay at its southern frontier bordering Cush.
native_notes.29:19: Hebrew hamon carries both the sense of wealth or abundance, as here and in 30:4, and teeming multitude or horde, as in 30:10, 30:15, 31:2, and 31:18.
native_notes.30:13: The Masoretic Hebrew names of the Egyptian cities in 30:13-18 are retained directly: Noph is Memphis, No is Thebes, Sin is Pelusium, and Aven is On or Heliopolis, vocalized as aven, wickedness, as a deliberate wordplay.
native_notes.30:16: Follows the qere tachul, will writhe, Qal imperfect 3fs of chul, rather than the ketiv spelling tachil. The closing phrase tsare yomam is an elliptical construct-before-adverb construction literally meaning adversaries by day.
native_notes.30:17: Hebrew wehennah is a feminine plural pronoun referring back to the cities Aven and Pi-beseth, since cities are grammatically feminine in Hebrew.
native_notes.30:18: The Masoretic text writes chasak with sin instead of chashak with shin, grow dark, an orthographic variant supported by the following reference to a covering cloud. Hebrew motot, yoke bars, follows the Masoretic vocalization rather than the Septuagint reading scepters.
native_notes.31:3: Hebrew avotim in 31:3, 31:10, and 31:14 is morphologically a plural of avot, dense or intertwined boughs, as in Ezekiel 19:11, though ancient versions render it clouds by connecting it to av.
native_notes.31:10: The Masoretic text shifts abruptly from second-person masculine singular gavahta, you towered, directly addressing the royal figure, to third-person masculine singular forms for the rest of the verse.
native_notes.31:14: Hebrew elehem is pointed with an initial tsere as the plural noun el or ayil with a suffix, their mighty ones or mighty trees, rather than the preposition alehem, to them.
native_notes.31:15: Hebrew ulpeh is a rare Pual-patterned stative or nominal form from the root alaph, meaning grew faint or wilted.
native_notes.31:17: Hebrew uzeroo literally means and its arm, referring collectively to the empire's military allies or supporters, which accounts for the plural verb yashevu, dwelt.
native_notes.32:2: The verb nidmeta is taken as Niphal of damah II ("be ruined/undone"), with "young lion of the nations" as vocative, since damah I ("resemble") is unattested elsewhere in Niphal and normally takes a preposition; alternatively, from damah I, "You have likened yourself to a young lion of the nations."
native_notes.32:5: Hebrew ramuteka is a hapax legomenon from the root rum ("be high"), literally "your height," denoting the monster's towering bulk or massive carcass.
native_notes.32:6: Hebrew tsafateka is a hapax legomenon from tsuf ("flow/overflow"), construed here as a second object ("your outflow") clarified by "with your blood"; alternatively, a construct phrase, "the land of your swimming."
native_notes.32:27: Translates the Masoretic Hebrew directly: me'arelim ("from among the uncircumcised") and avonotam ("their iniquities," a plural noun with a preceding 3fs verb).
native_notes.32:32: Translates the Masoretic Qere chittiti ("My terror"); the written Ketiv reads chittito ("his terror").
native_notes.33:12: Hebrew bah ("by it") is feminine singular, referring back unambiguously to feminine tsedeqah ("righteousness") rather than the nearer masculine resha ("wickedness").
native_notes.33:25: Hebrew al-haddam ("with the blood") is the cultic and dietary idiom for eating meat without draining its blood, prohibited in Leviticus 19:26.
native_notes.33:26: Hebrew literally reads "stood upon your sword" and uses a feminine plural verb form for "you have committed."
native_notes.33:30: Hebrew chad ("one") is an Aramaicized form of standard Hebrew echad, occurring only here in the Hebrew text of the Old Testament.
native_notes.33:32: Masoretic vocalization reads shir agavim ("a song of passionate love," echoing agavim in v. 31), followed by personal qualifiers describing a skilled singer and musician.
native_notes.34:2: The Hebrew verb ra'ah ('tend, shepherd, feed') creates wordplay with ro'im ('shepherds'): instead of tending the flock, Israel's leaders have been tending and feeding themselves (v. 3).
native_notes.34:12: The noun baqqarah ('looking after, inspection') occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible, and niphrashot ('scattered') is the sole Niphal occurrence of parash.
native_notes.34:16: The Masoretic Text reads 'I will destroy' (Hiphil imperfect of shamad), contrasting judgment on the oppressive sheep with care for the vulnerable; several ancient versions (including the Septuagint) instead reflect 'I will guard' (from shamar).
native_notes.34:18: The noun mishqa' ('clear water', literally 'settled water', from shaqa', 'sink/settle') and the noun mirpas in v. 19 ('what is muddied', from raphas) each appear only here in the Hebrew Bible.
native_notes.34:29: Literally 'a planting for a name,' meaning a renowned planting; the Masoretic Text reads leshem ('for renown'), whereas the Septuagint reflects 'of peace.'
native_notes.35:5: Literally 'poured out the sons of Israel onto the hands of the sword,' an idiom for delivering them over to slaughter; 'final punishment' translates 'avon qets, literally 'iniquity/punishment of the end.'
native_notes.35:6: The Hebrew clause 'im-lo' dam sane'ta (literally 'if you did not hate blood') is grammatically difficult and is taken causally here ('since you did not hate bloodshed'), contrasting with the affirmative oath particle 'im-lo' elsewhere.
native_notes.35:9: Following the Qere tashovnah ('will not be restored/return', Qal imperfect of shuv); the Ketiv teyshavnah (from yashav) reads 'will not be inhabited.'
native_notes.35:12: Following the Qere shamemu ('they have become desolate', 3rd-person plural Qal perfect of shamem), agreeing with 'the mountains of Israel'; the Ketiv reads the singular shamemah ('it has become desolate' or 'desolation').
native_notes.36:3: The forms shammot (an unusual infinitive construct of shamam used transitively, making desolate) and sha'oph (Qal infinitive absolute of sha'aph, crushing or trampling) function together with an indefinite subject; literally "upon the lip of a tongue" is a Hebrew idiom for gossip or slanderous talk.
native_notes.36:5: Literally "in order that its open pastureland for plunder," with an implied verb; the Masoretic vocalization migrashah points the word as the noun migrash (open or pastureland) with a feminine suffix, though some construe it as an Aramaizing infinitive of garash (to expel or empty).
native_notes.36:13: Here and in vv. 14-15, the Qere reads plural goyayikh ("your nations"), while the Ketiv reads singular goyekh ("your nation"); in v. 13 the Qere also reads standard feminine singular at ("you") for the archaic Ketiv spelling atti.
native_notes.36:14: The Qere reads teshakkeli (Piel of shakhal, "bereave"), matching vv. 12-13, whereas the Ketiv reads takhshili (from kashal, "cause to stumble"), matching the Hiphil verb takhshili in v. 15.
native_notes.37:9: The Hebrew noun ruach carries a deliberate triple wordplay across vv. 1-14, shifting between "Spirit" (vv. 1, 14), "breath" (vv. 5-6, 8-10), and "winds" (arba' ruchot, "four winds," v. 9).
native_notes.37:17: The form la'achadim is the rare plural of echad ("one"), literally "into ones," expressing complete unity; qarav is an unusual transitive imperative ("join together" or "bring near").
native_notes.37:22: The Qere reads plural yihyu ("they will be"), matching the plural verbs in the verse, while the Ketiv reads singular yihyeh ("it will be"), agreeing with the collective "one nation."
native_notes.37:23: The Masoretic text reads moshvoteihem ("their dwelling places"); the Septuagint reflects a different reading, meshuvoteihem ("their apostasies" or "backslidings").
native_notes.38:2: Hebrew nesi rosh (literally "prince of the head") is rendered here as "chief prince," with Meshech and Tubal paired as in 27:13 and 32:26; alternatively, taking rosh as a proper noun yields "prince of Rosh, Meshech, and Tubal."
native_notes.38:12: Hebrew tabbur literally means "navel," an idiom denoting the center or highest point of the land or earth (cf. Judges 9:37). The 2nd-person masculine singular suffix on yadekha ("your hand") shows that Gog's direct speech ends at v. 11.
native_notes.38:13: Hebrew kefireha literally means "its young lions," a recurring metaphor in Ezekiel for proud rulers or warriors (cf. 19:3; 32:2).
native_notes.38:18: Hebrew be'appi literally means "in My nose" or "in My nostrils," a vivid anatomical idiom for burning anger.
native_notes.39:2: The Piel verb shishetikha is a hapax legomenon of uncertain meaning; in this sequence of verbs it is understood as "lead you forward" or "drive you on"; a derivation from shesh ("six"), "leave a sixth part of you," has also been proposed.
native_notes.39:11: Masoretic meqom-sham qever literally reads "a place there of a grave" (i.e., a burial place there). The name Hamon-gog means "Multitude of Gog," anticipating the city name Hamonah ("Multitude") in v. 16.
native_notes.39:14: In meqabberim et-ha'overim et-hannotarim, the first et is the preposition "with" (joining the buriers with those passing through, as described in v. 15), while the second et marks the direct object "those left."
native_notes.39:25: Ketiv reads shevit ("captivity"), while Qere reads shevut ("fortunes" or "restoration," in the idiom "restore the fortunes of"); the translation follows the Qere.
native_notes.39:26: Masoretic venasu (pointed with sin and spelled without aleph) is the Qal of nasa ("bear"), matching Ezekiel's recurring idiom "bear disgrace" (cf. 16:52, 54); some emend to shin from nashah ("forget").
native_notes.40:8: The Masoretic Text preserves this measurement of the vestibule toward the house (one reed) alongside the eight-cubit measurement in v. 9. The phrase mehabbayit (literally 'from the house,' vv. 7-9) indicates the inner side facing the temple house.
native_notes.40:14: The Hebrew syntax is compressed and difficult: wayya'as ('he made,' Qal of 'asah) appears to mean 'he reckoned' or 'measured out,' and the second clause literally reads 'and to the jamb of the court, the gate all around.'
native_notes.40:15: Translated from the qere ha'iton ('the entrance,' a rare noun from 'atah, 'to come'); the ketiv hy'twn is a variant consonantal spelling.
native_notes.40:43: The rare dual noun shefattayim is uncertain in meaning, referring either to double-pronged hooks or to ledges fastened around the inside of the slaughtering area.
native_notes.40:44: The Masoretic Text literally reads 'chambers for singers' (lishkot sharim) and 'the east gate' (sha'ar haqqadim), whereas the Septuagint reads 'two chambers' and 'the south gate.'
native_notes.41:1: The Masoretic Text literally reads "the width of the tent," an unusual phrase echoing tabernacle language; the Septuagint diverges here.
native_notes.41:6: Hebrew literally reads "three and thirty times"; in light of the three stories in 41:7 this is often understood as three stories of thirty side rooms each.
native_notes.41:8: The Qere reads "foundations" (musdot), whereas the Ketiv spells the word with yod instead of waw. The rare term atsilah literally means "to the joint," often understood as six long cubits or up to the joining point of the side rooms.
native_notes.41:15: The Qere reads "and its galleries" (we-attiqeha, spelled with yod to match 41:16), whereas the Ketiv spells the stem with waw.
native_notes.41:20: The Masoretic Text places extraordinary scribal dots (puncta extraordinaria) over the final word "the temple hall" (hahekal), marking textual uncertainty, likely because 41:21 immediately begins with the same word.
native_notes.42:4: The Masoretic Text reads "a passage of one cubit" (derekh ammah achat), whereas the Septuagint reflects "a length of a hundred cubits."
native_notes.42:9: Two Ketiv/Qere variants occur here: the Qere redivides the first phrase as "and below these chambers" and reads the Hiphil participle "the entryway" (hammevi) where the Ketiv has the noun "the entrance" (hammavo).
native_notes.42:10: The Masoretic Text reads "toward the east" (derekh haqqadim), whereas the Septuagint reads "toward the south," anticipating the south chambers in 42:12.
native_notes.42:12: The rare word haginah ("matching") occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible; its exact sense is uncertain, though cognates suggest "corresponding," "suitable," or "directly opposite."
native_notes.42:16: The Qere reads "reeds" (qanim), aligning with 42:17-19, whereas the Ketiv reads "cubits" (ammot), which agrees with the Septuagint and the scale of chapters 40-41.
native_notes.43:3: MT reads first-person bebo'i ("when I came"), expressing Ezekiel's prophetic participation in the vision of Jerusalem's destruction (cf. ch. 9), whereas some Hebrew manuscripts and ancient versions read third-person "when He came."
native_notes.43:5: Hebrew ruach lacks the definite article here and may be read as "a spirit," "the Spirit," or "wind" (cf. 2:2).
native_notes.43:7: The direct object marker 'et precedes "the place of My throne" without a governing verb, functioning presentatively ("this is"). At the end of the verse, MT vocalizes bamotam ("their high places," used locatively or denoting royal funerary shrines), whereas repointing the consonants to bemotam yields "at their death."
native_notes.43:13: Hebrew cheq (lit. "bosom" or "hollow") denotes the recessed base or drainage gutter around the altar. MT gav ("back," "mound," or "pedestal") is retained here rather than emending to "height" (govah) with the Septuagint.
native_notes.43:15: Hebrew uses two related terms for the altar hearth: har'el and Qere 'ari'el (also in 43:16), where the Ketiv transposes the yod and 'alef ('r'yl) while the Qere reads 'ry'l.
native_notes.43:26: Hebrew umille'u yadav (lit. "and they shall fill its hands," with defective suffix spelling) applies the standard priestly consecration idiom ("fill the hand," cf. Exod 29:9) uniquely to the altar.
native_notes.44:3: The initial direct object marker 'et introduces "the prince" as a fronted topic ("As for the prince"). The Qere le'ekhol- binds "to eat" with maqqef to "bread" in defective spelling, whereas the Ketiv writes the Qal infinitive construct plene (l'kwl).
native_notes.44:7: MT reads third-person plural wayyaferu ("and they broke," Hiphil wayyiqtol of parar), shifting from second-person plural address; some ancient versions harmonize to second-person "you broke."
native_notes.44:18: Hebrew bayyaza' (lit. "in/with sweat," a hapax legomenon) refers to garments or belts that induce perspiration during priestly service.
native_notes.44:24: Two Ketiv/Qere variants occur here: Qere lemishpat ("for judgment") vs. Ketiv lshpt ("to judge," Qal infinitive construct), and Qere yishpetuhu ("they shall judge it," Qal imperfect) vs. Ketiv wshpthw ("and they shall judge it," Qal weqatal).
native_notes.44:28: The feminine singular verb wehayetah ("and it/this shall be") has no explicit subject, either functioning cataphorically to introduce "I am their inheritance" or agreeing by attraction with the feminine predicate noun nachalah ("inheritance").
native_notes.45:1: The unit of length is omitted in the Hebrew text here and in verses 3, 5, and 6 (likely cubits by comparison with 45:2); the noun "length" is also repeated resumptively around the numeral twenty-five thousand.
native_notes.45:3: The qere reads the masculine numeral "chamishah" ("five", matching the standard construction with "thousand"), whereas the ketiv writes the feminine form "chamesh".
native_notes.45:5: The qere reads the waw-consecutive Qal perfect "vehayah" ("shall belong"), whereas the ketiv reads the imperfect "yihyeh". The Masoretic Text explicitly reads "twenty chambers" ("esrim leshakot").
native_notes.45:12: The Masoretic Text lists three sub-weights totaling sixty shekels (20 + 25 + 15) for the mina, reflecting a sexagesimal weight standard.
native_notes.45:21: The Hebrew reads "shevu'ot yamim" (vocalized as plural of "shavua", literally "weeks of days"), functioning here in context as a seven-day period, matching "the seven days of the festival" in verse 23.
native_notes.46:9: The qere reads the singular Qal imperfect "yetse" ("he shall go out", agreeing with the singular subject), whereas the ketiv reads the plural "yets'u" ("they shall go out").
native_notes.46:15: The qere reads the Qal imperfect "ya'asu" ("they shall prepare"), whereas the ketiv reads the waw-consecutive Qal perfect "ve'asu" ("and they shall prepare").
native_notes.46:19: The qere reads the dual "bayyarkatayim" ("at the extreme rear"), whereas the ketiv reads "beyarkatam" (either "at their far end" or a defective dual spelling).
native_notes.46:22: The Qal passive participle "qeturot" is a biblical hapax legomenon, traditionally understood as "enclosed" or "unroofed" courts. The final word "mehuqtsa'ot" (Hophal participle, "set in the corners") carries Masoretic extraordinary points (puncta extraordinaria) above its letters.
native_notes.47:8: The Hophal participle "hammutsa'im" (from "yatsa", literally "those brought out / led forth") describes the temple waters discharging into the sea so that its waters are healed.
native_notes.47:9: The Hebrew uses the dual form "nachalayim" (literally "two rivers" or "double river") with a singular verb, emphasizing the great volume of the stream.
native_notes.47:10: The qere reads the Qal perfect "amedu" following "vehayah" ("will stand"), whereas the ketiv reads the Qal imperfect "ya'amdu".
native_notes.47:12: The qere reads the singular Qal perfect "vehayah" (agreeing with singular "its fruit"), whereas the ketiv reads the plural "vehayu".
native_notes.47:13: The demonstrative "geh" ("this") occurs only here in the Masoretic Text as a variant of "zeh" (cf. verse 15). "Two portions" renders the elliptic Hebrew "Yosef chavalim" (literally "Joseph, portions"), reflecting Ephraim and Manasseh.
native_notes.47:20: Literally "the entrance of Hamath," the same northern border town named "Lebo-hamath" in 48:1.
native_notes.48:8: The Hebrew text omits the unit of measurement throughout chapter 48; the figures are traditionally understood as cubits.
native_notes.48:11: Hebrew uses a collective singular Pual participle, literally 'the consecrated one,' in apposition to the plural 'priests.'
native_notes.48:14: Translates the qere (Hiphil imperfect, 'transfer'); the ketiv reads the Qal imperfect ('pass over'), making 'the best of the land' the grammatical subject.
native_notes.48:16: The Masoretic Text contains a written dittography of 'five' in the southern measurement that is marked as ketiv velo qere (written, not read) and therefore omitted in translation.
native_notes.48:28: The Hebrew form rendered 'to the brook' is pointed like the noun 'inheritance,' though in this southern border formula it represents 'brook/wadi' with a directional ending, referring to the Wadi of Egypt.
